themes.title: Planning for a better planet
themes.image_alt: Plan4Planet logo: a tree of gears and circuits with a city, crops and wind turbines at its roots
themes.label: Projects
themes.blurb: A changing climate demands hard decisions about where to look and what to do. Our newest thread brings AI planning and scheduling to Earth science: directing satellites and sensors to watch volcanoes and extreme heat, and connecting planning researchers with climate experts.

projects.name: Satellite & sensorweb scheduling
projects.text: With NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, we developed approaches for scheduling imaging across fleets of Earth-observing satellites, and for coordinating space and ground sensors into sensorwebs that monitor events such as volcanic eruptions.

projects.name: FAME-HEAT28: extreme heat at LA28
projects.text: Jim is consulting with JPL (2026–2027) on planning new space, air, and ground observations that reduce uncertainty in extreme-heat decisions for the LA 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

projects.name: Plan4Planet
projects.text: Jim's initiative to bring AI planning and reasoning researchers together with climate experts on the decisions a changing climate demands, starting with the Planning for a Better Planet AAAI Fall Symposium (November 5–7, 2026, Arlington, Virginia).

themes.title: Human-robot teamwork
themes.image_alt: A NAO humanoid robot on a desk while a student works at a computer
themes.blurb: How should robots and AI agents share work with people? We build scheduling approaches for mixed human-robot teams and test them with real people and real robots, measuring trust, fluency, and who should take the lead.

projects.name: CHAI: Cultivating Human-Agent Interactions
projects.text: As collaborative robots become commonplace, creating schedules for human-robot teamwork will be crucial. This project tested scheduling algorithms developed for robot teams on human-robot teams, using Rethink Robotics' Sawyer to study how people and robots complete tasks together, and how human autonomy affects a team's productivity.

projects.name: Human-Robot Trust
projects.text: How much a person trusts a robot shapes how they interact with it. Using a coin entrustment game (a variant of the prisoner's dilemma) and our NAO robot, we measured trust and cooperation as separate phenomena, comparing how people treat robots versus other humans.

projects.name: MAD about Fluency
projects.text: What makes a human-robot collaboration feel fluent? We built MAD-TN, a tool for measuring fluency, and used it to study human temporal uncertainty and the fluency of human-robot interactions.

projects.name: Improvisational Teamwork
projects.text: Simple temporal networks that let people and agents coordinate on the fly, plus analysis of how dynamic control holds up when uncertainty is skewed.

projects.name: PaWPal: Productivity and Wellness Pal
projects.text: College students often struggle to balance work with wellness. PaWPal, an Android app, used experience sampling to model when users are most likely to experience flow and to nudge them toward more productive, immersive work. It was the precursor to the campus-wide Workload and Health at Mudd (WHAM!) study.

themes.title: Plans that survive the real world
themes.image_alt: A simple temporal network diagram next to the 3D polytope of its possible schedules
themes.blurb: Robots slip and people run late. We develop the math and algorithms behind temporal plans that stay flexible, durable, and controllable when things don't go as expected.

projects.name: Probably-in-Control
projects.text: Sometimes scheduling uncertainty outstrips an agent's ability to control for it. We developed analytical tools for the “degree of controllability”: the likelihood that an agent, such as a robot, can still control for uncertainty caused by slippage or localization error.

projects.name: Ctrl-Alt-Repeat
projects.text: Dynamic control strategies for probabilistic simple temporal networks: deciding when to act as uncertain events unfold.

projects.name: PolyBots & Acrobotics
projects.text: The constraints in a temporal plan define a polytope bounding the space of possible schedules, and its geometry says something about the plan. PolyBots used geometric properties to quantify a plan's flexibility; Acrobotics introduced “durability,” a measure of a schedule's resilience to disturbances.

themes.title: Multi-robot coordination
themes.image_alt: Two students on the lab floor setting up a small wheeled robot inside a taped-off course
themes.blurb: When a team of robots shares a plan, every delay ripples. We study how robots can schedule robust interactions, and how much communication and rescheduling that really takes.

projects.name: Robot Brunch
projects.text: We want multi-robot plans that adapt to events beyond the robots' control, like slippage or sensor failures. This project introduced robustness, the likelihood that a multi-robot plan succeeds, and execution strategies that keep plans robust as they run.

projects.name: DREAM
projects.text: Keeping a multi-robot plan robust can take constant rescheduling and communication. Working with Jeremy Frank at NASA Ames, we measured the trade-offs between communication, rescheduling, and success rate, and developed DREAM, a single streamlined algorithm that balances robustness against computational and communication overhead.
